World.title: Almost 50 per cent of dementia cases could be prevented. This new advice tells us how
World.content:
NationalDementia Almost 50 per cent of dementia cases could be prevented. This new advice tells us how Kate Aubusson July 19, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Avoiding air pollution from fireplaces and vehicle emissions is among a suite of new dementia prevention recommendations from the World Health Organisation (WHO), which have not endorsed supplements or menopausal hormone therapy to cut the risk of cognitive decline. Up to 45 per cent of dementia risk could be prevented or delayed by eliminating modifiable risk factors including tobacco, alcohol, not exercising, diabetes and high blood pressure, according to the first update to the WHO’s dementia prevention guidelines in seven years. Estrogen therapy was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease in women with premature ovarian insufficiency. Getty Images But the WHO’s expert dementia panel, drawing on the latest evidence of dementia risk and effective treatments, stressed that individuals alone won’t make a dent in the prevalence of dementia without government action. “We know more today than ever before about what drives dementia risk, and these guidelines translate that knowledge into action,” said WHO director-general Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.



Related Article Science The five everyday products linked to nearly one-third of all deaths globally “Countries now have clear, evidence-based recommendations they can put into practice immediately to protect people’s cognitive health.” A healthy diet rich in leafy greens, berries, nuts and olive oil, and low in processed and ultra-processed foods, along with physical activity and daily cognitive stimulation, were among the most crucial dementia prevention strategies. The latter could be taking a course, learning a language, attending public lectures, reading and playing games: “things that actually challenge your brain. It’s not just doing the same crossword every day,” said Scientia Professor Kaarin Anstey, director of the UNSW Ageing Futures Institute and the only Australian on the WHO’s dementia panel. Anstey also stressed that reducing exposure to household and ambient air pollution, such as PM2.5 particulates from vehicle emissions, was important and warranted new conditional recommendations.



“What a lot of people don’t realise is that the risk isn’t just for those living next door to a polluting factory. A lot of us are exposed to air pollution living in cities,” she said. “The smoke produced from burning a fire in your fireplace can have negative health effects.” Conversely, the guidelines strongly recommended against vitamin and mineral supplements to reduce the risk of cognitive decline and dementia, specifically vitamins B and E, omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids and multivitamins and minerals. A potentially controversial update to the guidelines, Anstey said, was a conditional recommendation against menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) specifically for reducing the risk of cognitive decline or dementia in post menopausal women aged 65 years and older. There was also insufficient evidence for or against MHT for women experiencing premature ovarian insufficiency, early menopause or perimenopause for the specific purpose of reducing cognitive decline or dementia risk. The International Menopause Society does not recommend initiation of MHT for primary prevention of [Alzheimer’s Dementia] in naturally menopausal women, but it noted estrogen therapy was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease in women with premature ovarian insufficiency.



Related Article Healthcare Charlie’s dad died of a rare disease often misdiagnosed as depression “The evidence base for this is very messy,” Anstey said. “We’re basing these guidelines on the evidence through a very rigorous process. We look at the whole of the literature, its methodologies, and synthesise it all.” The new guidelines also found insufficient evidence to recommend interventions for depression, sleep, stroke, traumatic brain injury, vision impairment and HIV for the specific purpose of reducing dementia risk. Other key updates backed interventions to combat midlife obesity and overweight, hearing aids for people with hearing loss, and social engagement interventions to guard against loneliness and isolation. More than 57 million people live with dementia worldwide, and nearly 10 million people get newly diagnosed every year. Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia and is estimated to account for 60 to 70 per cent of cases.



Dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease, is Australia’s biggest killer, outstripping cardiovascular disease. An estimated 446,500 Australians will have dementia in 2026, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. “In order to achieve the reduction [of 45 per cent] we would have to eliminate the risk factors [obesity, insufficient activity], which is not going to happen,” Anstey said. “I think we can get some significant mitigation, but there needs to be whole-of-population interventions to really pull it down,” she said. “It has to be a whole-of-government response”. “We have to look at solutions at a societal level. This is not all down to the individual because there are social and commercial determinants of health, like access to and affordability of healthy food and exercise.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. World.title: Point to prove: Finals to arrive early with Izak Rankine to confront Collingwood
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 Point to prove: Finals to arrive early with Izak Rankine to confront Collingwood Peter Ryan July 19, 2026 — 7:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Collingwood and Adelaide have split their matches since Izak Rankine last played against the Pies.

Adem Yze needs to demand more from Richmond.

Tasmania Devils will enter the real world now they have announced their coach.

Could Max King ‘do a Charlie Curnow’?

Collingwood have been treating every game like a final since the bye. On Thursday night, after successive wins over Port Adelaide, Richmond, Gold Coast, North Melbourne and Carlton the eighth-placed Magpies finally get an opponent worthy of a final when they play an in-form Adelaide who sit fifth. It’s the first time the Magpies will have to contend with Izak Rankine in a Crows’ jumper since he was suspended from the finals for using a homophobic slur in the round 23 clash against Collingwood last year. The Crows will face Collingwood with Izak Rankine for the first time since he was suspended for using a homophobic slur. AFL Photos



The Magpies won last year’s qualifying final and the Crows won in round one to make it one win apiece since that fateful game but the match-winning Crow’s presence on Thursday night is significant. Rankine has put last year’s error behind him and has been building back to the form he showed at the Crows in the previous two seasons. On Friday night he was back to his best, his tackle and smother on Swans’ star Isaac Heeney in the final quarter on Friday night was a significant indication of his evolution as a player. Ferocious competitor Alex Neal-Bullen is the only Crows’ player putting more pressure on than the No.23. All eyes will be on him with the Magpies likely to send their cooling agent (or WS-23) Ed Allan to his side at stoppage. Allan was one of five Collingwood players with fewer than 30 games experience who played in the win over Carlton (who had seven).



It will be a battle within a battle as the competition’s two best teams at applying pressure prepare to wrestle like grizzly bears with the Crows needing to play a front half game to kick a winning score, particularly with Darcy Fogarty likely to miss through suspension. Brimming with confidence: Collingwood coach Craig McRae (left). AFL Photos The Magpies attack from defence more than the Crows with their scores from kick-ins becoming a problem for opponents. The Crows will need to be on guard for Jeremy Howe’s flat bullets into the centre and Nick Daicos’ give and go runs through the corridor causing damage. Some players don’t deserve the statistic they get for a kick-in, but the argument to not count the disposal on individual stat sheets doesn’t hold up when Howe or Daicos grab the footy. If they get the kick wrong, the chance is high it goes back over their head. If not, the Magpies can score.



Richmond’s excuses have worn thin Richmond were 63 points down at half-time against Hawthorn. The class gap was obvious. All anyone expected was some response. The opposite occurred as the Hawks waltzed around Richmond in the opening minutes of the second half as though the Tigers players were taking part in the Mannequin Challenge. Richmond were flat-footed and without spirit on Sunday against the Hawks AFL Photos via Getty Images It was unacceptable and inexcusable, regardless of Richmond’s injuries and experience.



Midway through the quarter the Tigers pressure rating was 138. The measure can be dependent on game style but Richmond has recorded the lowest pressure rating of any team this season. Adem Yze’s Tigers have not shown enough fight this season. AFL Photos Essendon’s effort was at the other end of the scale against the Giants after half-time which made the toothless Tigers’ performance even worse. The Bombers’ win put Richmond on the bottom of the ladder and to be honest, on Sunday, they looked the wooden spooners. Richmond laid 50 tackles and nine inside 50. The Bombers laid 69 and 18 inside 50. Their coach Adem Yze is a good character, but he needs to demand more from his team because his coaching career could depend on his team showing fight and applying pressure as much as some improvement on the injury front with the club searching for a new high-performance boss. Related Article Breaking

AFL 2026 Essendon climb off the bottom and snap losing streak with upset triumph over GWS



The 70-point loss to Hawthorn was the 17th time the Tigers have lost by 10 goals or more under Yze and the 15th time they have lost by that margin in the past 41 matches. They are the only team in the competition to not kick five unanswered goals this season. The Bombers kicked six unanswered against the Giants on Sunday. Josh Smillie has not yet played. Sam Lalor was impressive on limited minutes on Sunday. Sam Grjl, Harry Armstrong, Jonty Faull, Sam Cumming, Luke Trainor and Jasper Alger have shown glimpses of talent. But too often under Yze the Tigers have shown next to no fight with the premiership players who remain appearing to go through the motions. It’s not good enough. Ken Hinkley’s appointment will awaken the enemies Tasmania will enter the real world now they have announced Ken Hinkley as the club’s first coach.



Hinkley is a good call as he can attract and retain players as well as coaches and staff, having built a strong culture at Port Adelaide and maintaining many relationships from his time at Gold Coast and Geelong where he remains popular. But they will need his avuncular style because the rest of the competition will not be as accommodating as they may have been to date when they start putting their sign-on bonuses in front of their own talent. Tasmanians will get used to the many expressions of former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley who will become the Tassie Devils next coach. Artwork: Matt Willis. Photos: Getty Images Departing Giants’ CEO Dave Matthews telegraphed on 3AW on Saturday the uncompromising approach their opponents will take as they try to poach their talent with future Giants’ captain Tom Green one of their targets. “I don’t think it is a super attractive proposition to go and play in Tasmania,” Matthews said.



“It’s a nice place to visit. I don’t think it is an unbelievable place to have a career and live.” Given Matthews will consult to the AFL when his time at the Giants ends on a 20th team, international expansion and the upcoming collective bargaining agreement, his comments are likely to be on the lighter end of the doubts clubs will cast on the new club, who have admitted the training and administration centre will not be built when pre-season for 2028 starts while the Macquarie Point Stadium will host matches from 2031. And another thing, it’s timely the Devils have a media professional now on board because their executive needs to learn how to deal with breaking stories when they leak and not take offence when questions are asked about their progress. So far, their performance in that regard has been off the pace. The gloves are coming off.



Can Max King do a Charlie Curnow? That’s what the Saints will be hoping as their key forward prepares for a likely return on Sunday, July 26 against North Melbourne in his first game since June 30, 2024. The comparisons, in relation to time away from the AFL, are eerily similar. Curnow started his two years sidelined on June 30, 2019 and made his return against the Saints on July 30, 2021. Like King, Curnow had missed more than two seasons.



Luckless St Kilda Saints spearhead Max King. AFL Photos Like King, he returned with his team a slim chance to make finals but not a flag contender. The Blues had four games remaining when Curnow returned. The Saints have five. Curnow was 24 and had kicked 77 goals in 58 games. King is now 26 with 159 goals from 83 games. In that final four games in 2021, Curnow kicked just two goals but importantly he played 80 per cent game time in each match and set himself up for the preseason (coincidentally four current Saints, Jack Silvagni, Liam Stocker, Tom De Koning and Paddy Dow were in the Blues team for Curnow’s comeback match).



Curnow has played 108 matches and kicked 286 goals in close to five seasons since and won a Coleman Medal with Carlton. That is the type of result the Saints hope King might deliver. He is capable of repeating Curnow’s effort but all the work is now in front of him. They need him too as Cooper Sharman and Anthony Caminiti are not key forwards and crumbers such as Jack Higgins depend on forwards making contests to create ground balls inside 50. Geelong took 23 intercept marks against the Saints. St Kilda are still alive for a wildcard spot but watching King get through unscathed in the final five games to set up for next year would be equally satisfying. World.title: The Wallabies improved last year. We can’t say that about the last three weeks
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The Wallabies improved last year. We can’t say that about the last three weeks Paul Cully July 19, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rugby Australia (RA) has made some dubious claims of improvement, especially when high-performance director Peter Horne told this masthead at the start of July: “I’ve described last year as a good year, but a bad month.” Using that metric, the Wallabies have just had a stellar July – apart from the two weeks against Ireland and France. Loading That just doesn’t wash, and the Wallabies needed two wins out of three to plausibly claim they improved during July. There is no doubt that Joe Schmidt improved the Wallabies when he arrived, albeit off a historically low base following the Rugby World Cup shambles.



He is a quality coach, and he inherited a squad in disrepair. But that doesn’t give RA free rein to sympathetically mark its own homework when the punters know the Wallabies needed to beat an Ireland side at the end of their long season (see final item). Ryan Lonergan takes on the Italian defence in Perth. Getty Images The question mark over the Italy Test The Italians have been poor during the July series. They started with a 27-10 loss to Japan, fired up for a half against the All Blacks but ultimately faded, and then made multiple changes to their top side for the Wallabies Test. Their discipline has also been poor – two red cards and a ban for their coach Gonzalo Quesada in the past two weeks.



The Wallabies’ thumping 57-10 win therefore reflects a highly professional and at times powerful Australian performance, especially up front, but it will quickly move into the rearview mirror as the Wallabies start life under Les Kiss. The two selections the Wallabies have nailed There has been a lot of debate around some of the Wallabies’ selections, but Kiss will inherit a squad with a couple of real winners from the July Tests. Loading Halfback Ryan Lonergan and second-rower Josh Canham might seem like obvious selections at the end of July, but they weren’t at the start of the Test campaign. Lonergan is arguably the Wallabies’ most important player at the moment, given the control he brings to the ruck and his goalkicking ability. He’s a coach in the making.



Canham has long been an athlete of serious quality. Jeremy Williams has done a great job of being the “senior” partner in the second row, allowing Canham to play his natural game. Exodus to NZ raises Super Rugby AU questions The number of Australian players heading to New Zealand for the NPC continues to grow. Most of the Kiwi teams have revealed their squads over the past week, and it looks like more than 10 players have crossed the Tasman for the competition, which starts in two weeks. For example, Waratahs Clem Halaholo and Jack Barrett have joined Southland, Dan Botha is en route to Northland, the Brumbies’ Rory Scott has joined Tasman and Force prop Marley Pearce has landed at Otago. It is easy to see why the Australian Super Rugby clubs sanction these moves, but it arguably undermines the Super Rugby AU competition.



Related Article Australian rugby Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed Wallabies scars helping Rennie The All Blacks coach appeared pretty relaxed during a 14-minute press conference before the Ireland Test, and he now has most of the fickle New Zealand public onside after their 40-21 win at Eden Park on Saturday. Rennie might not necessarily enjoy the spotlight, but his communication has been good so far, and punters can connect what he is saying in the media to what they are seeing on the field. You cannot underestimate how important this is – previous coach Scott Robertson lost his way here. Rennie is a more rounded coach now than he was in Australia, But, there is a caveat to that big win against Ireland: the Irish have been messy in July, guilty of far too many unforced errors against the Wallabies, Japan and the All Blacks. They look well below their best. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Jean genies: Meet our low-key world record verifying gurus
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Jean genies: Meet our low-key world record verifying gurus Carolyn Webb July 19, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At first glance, a church hall at Yarraville in Melbourne’s inner west on Sunday resembled a jeans factory. There were 100 people wearing denim jeans, jackets, scarves and shirts, but it wasn’t a jeans commercial, or some religious worship of workwear pioneer Levi Strauss. Helen and John Taylor, sitting at front, with Pitchface community choir including ABC newsreader Tamara Oudyn (standing front, fourth from right) at Pilgrim Uniting Church hall in Yarraville. Penny Stephens It was the Pitchface community choir, sweetly singing 1980s and ′90s pop songs, in rehearsal for their concert this Saturday at St Kilda’s Palais Theatre – where they will attempt to break the world record for the most number of people wearing double denim in one place. With 100 people in the choir and 1700 ticket holders, so far, asked to wear all denim, the odds are good of smashing the previous record of 357 set in Tokyo in 2024.



The choir’s co-founder, ABC newsreader Tamara Oudyn, said attempting a world record seemed like a fun way to get the crowd involved. Who you gonna call? The Australian Book of Records founders John and Helen Taylor, centre, with Pitchface choir founders Harriet O’Donnell, Tamara Oudyn and sisters Tessa and Domenique Meyrick. Penny Stephens But who can you call to judge your record? Pitchface turned to Helen and John Taylor, who have quietly become popular verifiers through their website The Australian Book of Records. Do you claim to have the loudest burp, or the longest leg hair? The Taylors can verify that. The couple were in the desert near Broken Hill on August 23 last year to confirm that 6779 people smashed the world record for dancing to Tina Turner’s hit Nutbush City Limits.



Last November, at Melbourne’s Federation Square, Helen presented the certificate when 374 pipers played AC/DC’s Long Way To the Top, smashing the world record for largest bagpipe ensemble. In August 2025, at the Mundi Mundi Bash in Broken Hill, 6779 people set the world record for most number of people dancing the Nutbush. The Australian Book of Records The Taylors previously travelled the world for Shell, as ambassadors in fuel efficiency. They each hold more than 90 world records. John holds the record for the most number of times crossing the British mainland, between John O’Groats in Scotland and Lands End in Cornwall. But they love seeing others’ excitement at smashing records.



“We like to make people’s dreams come true,” John says. “People walk away feeling good about themselves.” Adjudicator Helen Taylor at Federation Square on November 12, 2025, holding the record certificate for world’s largest bagpipe ensemble. Right of her is Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece. The Australian Book of Records The Taylors aren’t paid; they only charge for expenses to cover costs, and their efforts have helped raise millions of dollars for charity. The 11 Nutbush record attempts, at Broken Hill and Birdsville, have raised $800,000 for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. Tamara Oudyn said Pitchface choir’s upcoming record attempt was inspired by a report in March this year of over 979 students raising awareness for the charity Fight MND by tipping icy water over their heads in Kew.



The world record was set for the number of people taking part in an ice bucket challenge. That event was adjudicated by Helen Taylor. “We love the cut of their jib,” Oudyn said, of the Taylors. “Imagine having that as a job? How fantastic.” “That sort of stuff is contagious – people all pulling in one direction together to achieve something.”



She said Pitchface choir, which backed Coldplay at Marvel Stadium, and sang at the Australian Open women’s tennis final, aims to bring joy and levity to others. Of Saturday’s concert, which guest stars Kate Miller-Heidke, Oudyn said: “It’s going to be a really fun, joyous reprieve from the world.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Man dies in car after cross-border pursuit
World.content:
A man has died in his car following a pursuit across the Queensland and NSW border, with an investigation now under away into the incident.

The man, believed to be a 25-year-old from Queensland, was allegedly armed with a firearm when he drove across the border at the Gold Coast about 1am on Sunday.

He was initially reported to police at Robina about 11.45pm, and was later found by officers on the side of West Burleigh Road. He evaded an attempt by officers to detain him, and crossed the border on the Gold Coast Highway.

Queensland Police reported the incident to NSW Police about 12.45am Sunday as he approached the border. NSW officers located the man on Sexton Hill Drive at Banora Point.

The man failed to stop when directed to do so and a police pursuit was initiated, continuing through multiple nearby suburbs before road spikes were successfully deployed twice in South Murwillumbah.

World.title: Essendon climb off the bottom and snap losing streak with upset triumph over GWS
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Essendon climb off the bottom and snap losing streak with upset triumph over GWS Ed Jackson , Nick Smart and Oliver Caffrey Updated July 19, 2026 — 7:16pm ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your daily wrap of footy news: Western Bulldogs heaped more pressure on Gold Coast with a nine-point win.

Hawthorn dined out on lowly Richmond at the MCG on Sunday.

Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus against Collingwood. Dons delight: Bombers end losing streak Essendon’s 99 days of pain are over after they pulled off the upset of the season to stun inconsistent GWS in a three-point thriller amid scenes of delirium at Marvel Stadium. Having won just one of their previous 30 games, the Bombers finally played with a sense of urgency to give Dean Solomon his first win in his 10th match as a caretaker coach, which includes three at Gold Coast in 2017. Sheer wonder: Jacob Farrow of the Bombers. Getty Images



Leading at every break, Essendon gave up their advantage twice in a frantic final term but hit back through clutch goals to Sullivan Robey and Peter Wright. With a wildcard spot still up for grabs, the Giants desperately tried to reclaim the lead in the dying stages, but Essendon hung on for a famous win - 10.7 (67) to 8.16 (64). It was Essendon’s first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they hadn’t won a game in Victoria since May 2025. View post on X The Bombers, who were ravaged by Brisbane last Sunday and had lost 12-straight matches, were given virtually no hope of matching it with the red-hot Giants.



But it does continue GWS’ baffling trend of struggling against lower-ranked opposition, but managing to dismantle last year’s grand finalists Brisbane and Geelong, as well as rampaging ladder-leaders Fremantle, amid their previous seven games. As well as the Bombers, GWS have dropped matches to St Kilda (twice) and West Coast. View post on X In a further concern for the Giants, they lost captain Toby Greene to a serious-looking quad injury during the third quarter. GWS were demolished in the clearances 45-28, as Essendon aces Zach Merrett (35 touches, one goal) and Sam Durham (25 disposals) rediscovered some form.



Further delighting the home crowd, former Essendon forward Jake Stringer endured a horror match in front of goal to finish with 0.7 on a wayward night for the Giants. The only concern for Essendon was young star Nate Caddy, who was sent to hospital due to an elevated heart rate. Caddy, who recently re-signed until the end of 2031 in a massive boost for the battling Bombers, didn’t return to the ground after quarter-time. The 21-year-old was looking weary speaking to Solomon and was taken straight to the rooms. Essendon football boss Daniel McPherson was seen engaged in serious conversation with medical staff on the bench while Caddy was assessed underneath Marvel Stadium. He was soon ruled out with illness in the second quarter, with Essendon later detailing the heart issues.



The result could prove costly for GWS, who would have jumped into 10th and a wildcard spot, had they beaten the Bombers. It also lifted Essendon to 17th, sending Richmond to the bottom of the ladder. View post on X AAP, more to come



Bontempelli stars for Dogs, Gold Coast lose eight straight The Western Bulldogs have heaped more pressure on Gold Coast with a nine-point win over the Suns at People First Stadium. A five-goals-to-none third quarter was the game-breaker after an arm wrestle of a first half in blustery conditions as the Bulldogs ran out 11.11 (77) to 9.14 (68) winners on Sunday. The defeat extends Gold Coast’s losing run to eight matches and leaves their outside hopes of a top 10 finish seemingly extinguished. Victory lifted the Bulldogs to seventh on the ladder.



Arthur Jones shows some dash for the Bulldogs. via Getty Images In a team shorn of Tom Liberatore (soreness) and Riley Garcia (hamstring tightness) and missing Bailey Dale for the first time since 2020, superstar Marcus Bontempelli was a standout. The Bulldogs’ captain ended the game with three goals, 23 disposals, four tackles and five clearances. Matthew Kennedy was the other multiple goalkicker for the visitors, with three, while Bailey Humphrey was busy with 29 disposals and 765 metres gained. For the Suns, Christian Petracca and Leo Lombard kicked two goals each while Touk Miller (39 disposals, five tackles, nine clearances) and Matt Rowell (26 disposals, 11 tackles and eight clearances) were strong in a beaten team.



Suns spearhead Ben King had a tough day, kicking 1.4 and failing to haul in a late mark that could have set up a grandstand finish. AAP Watson and Lewis pile on goals as Hawthorn destroy lowly Tigers Hawthorn have returned to third on the AFL ladder with a major percentage boost thanks to a brutal 70-point demolition of lowly Richmond at the MCG. The Hawks went into the clash sitting sixth after other results this weekend, but their 18.14 (122) to 6.16 (52) thrashing of the Tigers made a major statement and lifted them back into the top four.



Sunday’s final margin flattered Richmond after they kicked several late consolation goals once Hawthorn eased off in the final term. They had led by as much as 87 points during the third quarter. Pointing the way to a win: Hawthorn’s Nick Watson. AFL Photos Uncontracted Hawk Mitch Lewis dominated up forward with five goals, all in the first half. Goalsneak Nick Watson matched him by also kicking five goals in a stunning first-half performance.



The only injury concern for the Hawks was Jack Ginnivan, who was pulled at half-time with the club citing “back soreness.” For Richmond, it was a sour way to commemorate triple premiership player Dion Prestia’s 250th game. The only positive was veteran Tom Lynch finally kicking his 500th goal late in the final term after several weeks stuck on 499. Tiger Taj Hotton failed to finish the game after suffering an ankle injury, while fellow youngster Steely Green finished the match under a HIA. Jarman Impey is fleet of foot and kicks a running goal on Sunday. AFL Photos



Watson, who was back from a two-week injury lay-off, picked up where he left off by kicking the first goal mid-way through the first term after a pedestrian start by both teams. He was able to slot a second goal in the opening quarter but was upstaged by a rampaging Lewis, who kicked three in the first 30 minutes. Lewis would have had four goals by quarter-time had his set shot after the siren not narrowly missed. But Lewis didn’t have to wait too long for his fourth – which came early in the second term – on his way to five majors. The hapless Tigers went goalless in the first term, and were cruelly denied what would have been a brilliant Seth Campbell goal late in the term by an ARC overrule.



Richmond supporters had to wait until the ninth minute of the second quarter to cheer their side’s first major, which came courtesy of Patrick Retschko. View post on X The Tigers had two in a minute after Mykelti Lefau kicked truly, but any joy was short-lived as Hawthorn piled on the next six. Hawthorn led by a whopping 63 points at the main break, their largest halftime lead in five seasons under coach Sam Mitchell. The Hawks threatened to blow the margin beyond 100 points in the third term before the Tigers were able to make the scoreline more respectable by the final siren.



AAP McKay could play through injury for Carlton Scott Spits, Danny Russell Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus after an awkward clash that commentators described as innocuous-looking against Collingwood at the MCG on Saturday night. Scans on Sunday confirmed the prognosis for McKay, who was forced from the field early in the Blues’ 21-point loss to the Magpies that has effectively ruled Carlton out of the wildcard race.



McKay bumped knees with teammate Sam Walsh early in the first quarter. Despite the benign nature of the impact, McKay was unable to run and took himself from the ground. Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a meniscus tear. AFL Photos via Getty Images His absence left the Carlton forward line short on potency. The Blues said midfielder Adam Cerra, who experienced hamstring tightness and was withdrawn in the second quarter, had not suffered a strain. Carlton said McKay and Cerra would be tested and both may play against Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium next Saturday. Carlton’s caretaker coach Josh Fraser would not be drawn on the severity of McKay’s injury.



“Those ones can sometimes look worse than what they appear,” Fraser said after the match. “I don’t know. I haven’t received any more information on it.” Fox Footy commentator David King was perplexed by McKay’s injury. “No one is questioning whether he is injured or not,” he said. “We are just wondering if it is a pain issue or is it a structural issue. When it has such an influence on the group, it changes six or seven roles in the team, and they were right in the game.” Collingwood coach Craig McRae agreed McKay’s absence for most of the night aided an undermanned Magpies back line. World.title: ‘Witch’ troll truck back on road, set to haunt Spring Street
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD ‘Witch’ troll truck back on road, set to haunt Spring Street Fiona Byrne and John Buckley Updated July 19, 2026 — 7:58pm ,first published 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Double, double toil and trouble … the notorious troll truck featuring divisive billboard s that target Premier Jacinta Allan has returned to Melbourne streets. The truck, which as first reported by The Age was ordered off the road earlier this month after being issued with a defect notice by police, was spotted by CBD late on Friday turning from Exhibition Street into Bourke Street and trundling towards Parliament House with the slogan “It’s time to get rid of this witch” and its doctored image of Allan in full view. The notorious billboard truck with an ad that depicts Jacinta Allan as a witch is back on the streets of the CBD, as seen on Friday evening. Fiona Byrne The billboard truck, best known for advertising the Gotham City brothel on its screens, was issued with a defect notice related to the advertising screens and ordered off the road for inspection on July 8. The notice followed a complaint to police by a member of the public in April. The compliance issue was dropped and the vehicle deemed fully roadworthy by VicRoads last week.





“Police have been advised the truck was presented to VicRoads for inspection and the vehicle was deemed roadworthy. As such, police will not be taking any further action in respect to the vehicle.” An additional slogan has appeared on the controversial billboard truck reading, “Truck stays! Witch needs to go!” The defect notice had demanded the three large LED display screens on the vehicle be removed, and an accompanying email from police explained the complaint from the community member occurred before the anti-Labor ads started appearing on the screens. “Instead of worrying about fixing up this state, they’re busy picking on little businesses like me and everybody else who wants to speak out about this government by advertising on the truck,” Puleo fumed to CBD on Sunday. “There was never anything wrong with the truck. We’ve been told by a police officer that issued the notice that Vic Pol won’t hassle us again and won’t take instructions from other authorities. Jacinta should spend her energy on finding $15 billion and helping businesses and family people rather than giving herself a pay rise.”



Bezos slips in and orders a negroni

Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez, are in Australia – Sydney to be exact. For what purpose, we don’t know. But if nothing else, how the world’s fourth-richest person chooses to spend his time in the Emerald City has made for some good gawking. After being seen on Friday out for lunch at upmarket restaurant Mimi’s, in Coogee, Bezos was spotted that evening slipping into the Park Hyatt bar, where he was photographed by a CBD spy with what appeared to be a negroni. The billionaire Amazon founder, clad in black and sporting Cuban-heeled boots, was in the company of an unshaven, yet-to-be-identified man. Jeff Bezos spotted at the Park Hyatt bar in Sydney. Which is to say, setting aside transport and accommodation, Bezos has been living much like the rest of us.



If Sánchez’s Instagram is anything to go by, the pair may well be staying at the Park Hyatt, whose 350-square-metre Sydney Suite bears a striking resemblance to the balcony Sánchez shared a photo of to her 1.1 million followers on Sunday morning. The suite’s nightly rate isn’t listed by the Hyatt, but reportedly starts at about $21,000. Then there’s the transport. Flight-tracking data shows that one plane widely reported as belonging to Bezos, an ultra-luxury Gulfstream G700 private jet, landed in Sydney at 1.15pm on Friday after flying from the Pacific. Bezos, whose net worth is valued by Forbes at roughly $US260 billion ($372 billion), reportedly owns four private jets. Patrons at Mimi’s in Coogee were surprised to see Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sáchez Bezos, on Friday. Just what the pair are doing in Australia, though – and whether they will visit Melbourne – remains a mystery. Amazon does decent business in this market, and is among the tech giants jockeying to build data centres in Australia. The company already operates more than a dozen on Australian shores, and last year beat Elon Musk’s Starlink to secure a multimillion-dollar contract with the National Broadband Network to offer satellite internet to rural and regional Australians. Amazon Australia didn’t respond to a request for comment by deadline. So our guess is Bezos, who no longer leads the company as chief executive but remains its executive chairman, would surely have a few meetings in the diary, holiday or not.



Where’s Barnaby? Last week was a big one for One Nation. It was revealed the Senate’s perennial cooker Malcolm Roberts had described Alex Jones, a fountain of conspiracy theories including that the Sandy Hook school shooting was a false flag, as “a beacon of hope around the world”. Then came leader Pauline Hanson’s Mediterranean sojourn with billionaire Gina Rinehart. Which was topped off with a Hanson podcast appearance alongside the controversial far-right freak show Tommy Robinson, who’s proved too freaky even for UK Reform leader Nigel Farage, and has been dubbed a “thug” by Andrew Bolt. One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce with party leader Pauline Hanson in May. Alex Ellinghausen So when our colleagues revealed late last week that Hanson and Barnaby Joyce were in “constant disagreement”, there was always going to be some forensic tea leaves analysis. Joyce and One Nation, of course, insisted the former Nationals leader and his new boss have a trusting relationship.



Such was the case over the weekend when attention turned to the absence of Joyce’s name from the “team” page on the One Nation website, and the absence of the party name on Joyce’s own website. It’s unclear if Joyce ever made it onto the One Nation website or it’s been changed. Of course, as with anything One Nation, our guess was the omission would probably have more to do with a lack of professionalism and short staff numbers than, say, a looming split. But then again, who knows. When reached on Sunday, Joyce was “trying to get a pump on”, which we took to mean exercising, maybe lifting weights. He was exasperated by this masthead’s reporting last week, which revealed disagreements between him and Hanson. “Premised on what?” he asked. When asked about the absence of his name from the One Nation website, he said there was nothing to it. Pleasure to be of service clearing that one up. World.title: Point to prove: Finals to arrive early with Izak Rankine to confront Collingwood
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 Point to prove: Finals to arrive early with Izak Rankine to confront Collingwood Peter Ryan July 19, 2026 — 7:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Collingwood and Adelaide have split their matches since Izak Rankine last played against the Pies.

Adem Yze needs to demand more from Richmond.

Tasmania Devils will enter the real world now they have announced their coach.

Could Max King ‘do a Charlie Curnow’?

Collingwood have been treating every game like a final since the bye. On Thursday night, after successive wins over Port Adelaide, Richmond, Gold Coast, North Melbourne and Carlton the eighth-placed Magpies finally get an opponent worthy of a final when they play an in-form Adelaide who sit fifth. It’s the first time the Magpies will have to contend with Izak Rankine in a Crows’ jumper since he was suspended from the finals for using a homophobic slur in the round 23 clash against Collingwood last year. The Crows will face Collingwood with Izak Rankine for the first time since he was suspended for using a homophobic slur. AFL Photos



The Magpies won last year’s qualifying final and the Crows won in round one to make it one win apiece since that fateful game but the match-winning Crow’s presence on Thursday night is significant. Rankine has put last year’s error behind him and has been building back to the form he showed at the Crows in the previous two seasons. On Friday night he was back to his best, his tackle and smother on Swans’ star Isaac Heeney in the final quarter on Friday night was a significant indication of his evolution as a player. Ferocious competitor Alex Neal-Bullen is the only Crows’ player putting more pressure on than the No.23. All eyes will be on him with the Magpies likely to send their cooling agent (or WS-23) Ed Allan to his side at stoppage. Allan was one of five Collingwood players with fewer than 30 games experience who played in the win over Carlton (who had seven).



It will be a battle within a battle as the competition’s two best teams at applying pressure prepare to wrestle like grizzly bears with the Crows needing to play a front half game to kick a winning score, particularly with Darcy Fogarty likely to miss through suspension. Brimming with confidence: Collingwood coach Craig McRae (left). AFL Photos The Magpies attack from defence more than the Crows with their scores from kick-ins becoming a problem for opponents. The Crows will need to be on guard for Jeremy Howe’s flat bullets into the centre and Nick Daicos’ give and go runs through the corridor causing damage. Some players don’t deserve the statistic they get for a kick-in, but the argument to not count the disposal on individual stat sheets doesn’t hold up when Howe or Daicos grab the footy. If they get the kick wrong, the chance is high it goes back over their head. If not, the Magpies can score.



Richmond’s excuses have worn thin Richmond were 63 points down at half-time against Hawthorn. The class gap was obvious. All anyone expected was some response. The opposite occurred as the Hawks waltzed around Richmond in the opening minutes of the second half as though the Tigers players were taking part in the Mannequin Challenge. Richmond were flat-footed and without spirit on Sunday against the Hawks AFL Photos via Getty Images It was unacceptable and inexcusable, regardless of Richmond’s injuries and experience.



Midway through the quarter the Tigers pressure rating was 138. The measure can be dependent on game style but Richmond has recorded the lowest pressure rating of any team this season. Adem Yze’s Tigers have not shown enough fight this season. AFL Photos Essendon’s effort was at the other end of the scale against the Giants after half-time which made the toothless Tigers’ performance even worse. The Bombers’ win put Richmond on the bottom of the ladder and to be honest, on Sunday, they looked the wooden spooners. Richmond laid 50 tackles and nine inside 50. The Bombers laid 69 and 18 inside 50. Their coach Adem Yze is a good character, but he needs to demand more from his team because his coaching career could depend on his team showing fight and applying pressure as much as some improvement on the injury front with the club searching for a new high-performance boss. Related Article Breaking

AFL 2026 Essendon climb off the bottom and snap losing streak with upset triumph over GWS



The 70-point loss to Hawthorn was the 17th time the Tigers have lost by 10 goals or more under Yze and the 15th time they have lost by that margin in the past 41 matches. They are the only team in the competition to not kick five unanswered goals this season. The Bombers kicked six unanswered against the Giants on Sunday. Josh Smillie has not yet played. Sam Lalor was impressive on limited minutes on Sunday. Sam Grjl, Harry Armstrong, Jonty Faull, Sam Cumming, Luke Trainor and Jasper Alger have shown glimpses of talent. But too often under Yze the Tigers have shown next to no fight with the premiership players who remain appearing to go through the motions. It’s not good enough. Ken Hinkley’s appointment will awaken the enemies Tasmania will enter the real world now they have announced Ken Hinkley as the club’s first coach.



Hinkley is a good call as he can attract and retain players as well as coaches and staff, having built a strong culture at Port Adelaide and maintaining many relationships from his time at Gold Coast and Geelong where he remains popular. But they will need his avuncular style because the rest of the competition will not be as accommodating as they may have been to date when they start putting their sign-on bonuses in front of their own talent. Tasmanians will get used to the many expressions of former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley who will become the Tassie Devils next coach. Artwork: Matt Willis. Photos: Getty Images Departing Giants’ CEO Dave Matthews telegraphed on 3AW on Saturday the uncompromising approach their opponents will take as they try to poach their talent with future Giants’ captain Tom Green one of their targets. “I don’t think it is a super attractive proposition to go and play in Tasmania,” Matthews said.



“It’s a nice place to visit. I don’t think it is an unbelievable place to have a career and live.” Given Matthews will consult to the AFL when his time at the Giants ends on a 20th team, international expansion and the upcoming collective bargaining agreement, his comments are likely to be on the lighter end of the doubts clubs will cast on the new club, who have admitted the training and administration centre will not be built when pre-season for 2028 starts while the Macquarie Point Stadium will host matches from 2031. And another thing, it’s timely the Devils have a media professional now on board because their executive needs to learn how to deal with breaking stories when they leak and not take offence when questions are asked about their progress. So far, their performance in that regard has been off the pace. The gloves are coming off.



Can Max King do a Charlie Curnow? That’s what the Saints will be hoping as their key forward prepares for a likely return on Sunday, July 26 against North Melbourne in his first game since June 30, 2024. The comparisons, in relation to time away from the AFL, are eerily similar. Curnow started his two years sidelined on June 30, 2019 and made his return against the Saints on July 30, 2021. Like King, Curnow had missed more than two seasons.



Luckless St Kilda Saints spearhead Max King. AFL Photos Like King, he returned with his team a slim chance to make finals but not a flag contender. The Blues had four games remaining when Curnow returned. The Saints have five. Curnow was 24 and had kicked 77 goals in 58 games. King is now 26 with 159 goals from 83 games. In that final four games in 2021, Curnow kicked just two goals but importantly he played 80 per cent game time in each match and set himself up for the preseason (coincidentally four current Saints, Jack Silvagni, Liam Stocker, Tom De Koning and Paddy Dow were in the Blues team for Curnow’s comeback match).



Curnow has played 108 matches and kicked 286 goals in close to five seasons since and won a Coleman Medal with Carlton. That is the type of result the Saints hope King might deliver. He is capable of repeating Curnow’s effort but all the work is now in front of him. They need him too as Cooper Sharman and Anthony Caminiti are not key forwards and crumbers such as Jack Higgins depend on forwards making contests to create ground balls inside 50. Geelong took 23 intercept marks against the Saints. St Kilda are still alive for a wildcard spot but watching King get through unscathed in the final five games to set up for next year would be equally satisfying. World.title: The Wallabies improved last year. We can’t say that about the last three weeks
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionWallabies The Wallabies improved last year. We can’t say that about the last three weeks Paul Cully July 19, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rugby Australia (RA) has made some dubious claims of improvement, especially when high-performance director Peter Horne told this masthead at the start of July: “I’ve described last year as a good year, but a bad month.” Using that metric, the Wallabies have just had a stellar July – apart from the two weeks against Ireland and France. Loading That just doesn’t wash, and the Wallabies needed two wins out of three to plausibly claim they improved during July. There is no doubt that Joe Schmidt improved the Wallabies when he arrived, albeit off a historically low base following the Rugby World Cup shambles.



He is a quality coach, and he inherited a squad in disrepair. But that doesn’t give RA free rein to sympathetically mark its own homework when the punters know the Wallabies needed to beat an Ireland side at the end of their long season (see final item). Ryan Lonergan takes on the Italian defence in Perth. Getty Images The question mark over the Italy Test The Italians have been poor during the July series. They started with a 27-10 loss to Japan, fired up for a half against the All Blacks but ultimately faded, and then made multiple changes to their top side for the Wallabies Test. Their discipline has also been poor – two red cards and a ban for their coach Gonzalo Quesada in the past two weeks.



The Wallabies’ thumping 57-10 win therefore reflects a highly professional and at times powerful Australian performance, especially up front, but it will quickly move into the rearview mirror as the Wallabies start life under Les Kiss. The two selections the Wallabies have nailed There has been a lot of debate around some of the Wallabies’ selections, but Kiss will inherit a squad with a couple of real winners from the July Tests. Loading Halfback Ryan Lonergan and second-rower Josh Canham might seem like obvious selections at the end of July, but they weren’t at the start of the Test campaign. Lonergan is arguably the Wallabies’ most important player at the moment, given the control he brings to the ruck and his goalkicking ability. He’s a coach in the making.



Canham has long been an athlete of serious quality. Jeremy Williams has done a great job of being the “senior” partner in the second row, allowing Canham to play his natural game. Exodus to NZ raises Super Rugby AU questions The number of Australian players heading to New Zealand for the NPC continues to grow. Most of the Kiwi teams have revealed their squads over the past week, and it looks like more than 10 players have crossed the Tasman for the competition, which starts in two weeks. For example, Waratahs Clem Halaholo and Jack Barrett have joined Southland, Dan Botha is en route to Northland, the Brumbies’ Rory Scott has joined Tasman and Force prop Marley Pearce has landed at Otago. It is easy to see why the Australian Super Rugby clubs sanction these moves, but it arguably undermines the Super Rugby AU competition.



Related Article Australian rugby Wallabies player ratings: How the men in gold performed Wallabies scars helping Rennie The All Blacks coach appeared pretty relaxed during a 14-minute press conference before the Ireland Test, and he now has most of the fickle New Zealand public onside after their 40-21 win at Eden Park on Saturday. Rennie might not necessarily enjoy the spotlight, but his communication has been good so far, and punters can connect what he is saying in the media to what they are seeing on the field. You cannot underestimate how important this is – previous coach Scott Robertson lost his way here. Rennie is a more rounded coach now than he was in Australia, But, there is a caveat to that big win against Ireland: the Irish have been messy in July, guilty of far too many unforced errors against the Wallabies, Japan and the All Blacks. They look well below their best. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Jean genies: Meet our low-key world record verifying gurus
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Jean genies: Meet our low-key world record verifying gurus Carolyn Webb July 19, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At first glance, a church hall at Yarraville in Melbourne’s inner west on Sunday resembled a jeans factory. There were 100 people wearing denim jeans, jackets, scarves and shirts, but it wasn’t a jeans commercial, or some religious worship of workwear pioneer Levi Strauss. Helen and John Taylor, sitting at front, with Pitchface community choir including ABC newsreader Tamara Oudyn (standing front, fourth from right) at Pilgrim Uniting Church hall in Yarraville. Penny Stephens It was the Pitchface community choir, sweetly singing 1980s and ′90s pop songs, in rehearsal for their concert this Saturday at St Kilda’s Palais Theatre – where they will attempt to break the world record for the most number of people wearing double denim in one place. With 100 people in the choir and 1700 ticket holders, so far, asked to wear all denim, the odds are good of smashing the previous record of 357 set in Tokyo in 2024.



The choir’s co-founder, ABC newsreader Tamara Oudyn, said attempting a world record seemed like a fun way to get the crowd involved. Who you gonna call? The Australian Book of Records founders John and Helen Taylor, centre, with Pitchface choir founders Harriet O’Donnell, Tamara Oudyn and sisters Tessa and Domenique Meyrick. Penny Stephens But who can you call to judge your record? Pitchface turned to Helen and John Taylor, who have quietly become popular verifiers through their website The Australian Book of Records. Do you claim to have the loudest burp, or the longest leg hair? The Taylors can verify that. The couple were in the desert near Broken Hill on August 23 last year to confirm that 6779 people smashed the world record for dancing to Tina Turner’s hit Nutbush City Limits.



Last November, at Melbourne’s Federation Square, Helen presented the certificate when 374 pipers played AC/DC’s Long Way To the Top, smashing the world record for largest bagpipe ensemble. In August 2025, at the Mundi Mundi Bash in Broken Hill, 6779 people set the world record for most number of people dancing the Nutbush. The Australian Book of Records The Taylors previously travelled the world for Shell, as ambassadors in fuel efficiency. They each hold more than 90 world records. John holds the record for the most number of times crossing the British mainland, between John O’Groats in Scotland and Lands End in Cornwall. But they love seeing others’ excitement at smashing records.



“We like to make people’s dreams come true,” John says. “People walk away feeling good about themselves.” Adjudicator Helen Taylor at Federation Square on November 12, 2025, holding the record certificate for world’s largest bagpipe ensemble. Right of her is Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece. The Australian Book of Records The Taylors aren’t paid; they only charge for expenses to cover costs, and their efforts have helped raise millions of dollars for charity. The 11 Nutbush record attempts, at Broken Hill and Birdsville, have raised $800,000 for the Royal Flying Doctor Service. Tamara Oudyn said Pitchface choir’s upcoming record attempt was inspired by a report in March this year of over 979 students raising awareness for the charity Fight MND by tipping icy water over their heads in Kew.



The world record was set for the number of people taking part in an ice bucket challenge. That event was adjudicated by Helen Taylor. “We love the cut of their jib,” Oudyn said, of the Taylors. “Imagine having that as a job? How fantastic.” “That sort of stuff is contagious – people all pulling in one direction together to achieve something.”



She said Pitchface choir, which backed Coldplay at Marvel Stadium, and sang at the Australian Open women’s tennis final, aims to bring joy and levity to others. Of Saturday’s concert, which guest stars Kate Miller-Heidke, Oudyn said: “It’s going to be a really fun, joyous reprieve from the world.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Man dies in car after cross-border pursuit
World.content:
A man has died in his car following a pursuit across the Queensland and NSW border, with an investigation now under away into the incident.

The man, believed to be a 25-year-old from Queensland, was allegedly armed with a firearm when he drove across the border at the Gold Coast about 1am on Sunday.

He was initially reported to police at Robina about 11.45pm, and was later found by officers on the side of West Burleigh Road. He evaded an attempt by officers to detain him, and crossed the border on the Gold Coast Highway.

Queensland Police reported the incident to NSW Police about 12.45am Sunday as he approached the border. NSW officers located the man on Sexton Hill Drive at Banora Point.

The man failed to stop when directed to do so and a police pursuit was initiated, continuing through multiple nearby suburbs before road spikes were successfully deployed twice in South Murwillumbah.

World.title: Essendon climb off the bottom and snap losing streak with upset triumph over GWS
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Essendon climb off the bottom and snap losing streak with upset triumph over GWS Ed Jackson , Nick Smart and Oliver Caffrey Updated July 19, 2026 — 7:16pm ,first published 4:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

In today’s AFL Briefing, your daily wrap of footy news: Western Bulldogs heaped more pressure on Gold Coast with a nine-point win.

Hawthorn dined out on lowly Richmond at the MCG on Sunday.

Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus against Collingwood. Dons delight: Bombers end losing streak Essendon’s 99 days of pain are over after they pulled off the upset of the season to stun inconsistent GWS in a three-point thriller amid scenes of delirium at Marvel Stadium. Having won just one of their previous 30 games, the Bombers finally played with a sense of urgency to give Dean Solomon his first win in his 10th match as a caretaker coach, which includes three at Gold Coast in 2017. Sheer wonder: Jacob Farrow of the Bombers. Getty Images



Leading at every break, Essendon gave up their advantage twice in a frantic final term but hit back through clutch goals to Sullivan Robey and Peter Wright. With a wildcard spot still up for grabs, the Giants desperately tried to reclaim the lead in the dying stages, but Essendon hung on for a famous win - 10.7 (67) to 8.16 (64). It was Essendon’s first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they hadn’t won a game in Victoria since May 2025. View post on X The Bombers, who were ravaged by Brisbane last Sunday and had lost 12-straight matches, were given virtually no hope of matching it with the red-hot Giants.



But it does continue GWS’ baffling trend of struggling against lower-ranked opposition, but managing to dismantle last year’s grand finalists Brisbane and Geelong, as well as rampaging ladder-leaders Fremantle, amid their previous seven games. As well as the Bombers, GWS have dropped matches to St Kilda (twice) and West Coast. View post on X In a further concern for the Giants, they lost captain Toby Greene to a serious-looking quad injury during the third quarter. GWS were demolished in the clearances 45-28, as Essendon aces Zach Merrett (35 touches, one goal) and Sam Durham (25 disposals) rediscovered some form.



Further delighting the home crowd, former Essendon forward Jake Stringer endured a horror match in front of goal to finish with 0.7 on a wayward night for the Giants. The only concern for Essendon was young star Nate Caddy, who was sent to hospital due to an elevated heart rate. Caddy, who recently re-signed until the end of 2031 in a massive boost for the battling Bombers, didn’t return to the ground after quarter-time. The 21-year-old was looking weary speaking to Solomon and was taken straight to the rooms. Essendon football boss Daniel McPherson was seen engaged in serious conversation with medical staff on the bench while Caddy was assessed underneath Marvel Stadium. He was soon ruled out with illness in the second quarter, with Essendon later detailing the heart issues.



The result could prove costly for GWS, who would have jumped into 10th and a wildcard spot, had they beaten the Bombers. It also lifted Essendon to 17th, sending Richmond to the bottom of the ladder. View post on X AAP, more to come



Bontempelli stars for Dogs, Gold Coast lose eight straight The Western Bulldogs have heaped more pressure on Gold Coast with a nine-point win over the Suns at People First Stadium. A five-goals-to-none third quarter was the game-breaker after an arm wrestle of a first half in blustery conditions as the Bulldogs ran out 11.11 (77) to 9.14 (68) winners on Sunday. The defeat extends Gold Coast’s losing run to eight matches and leaves their outside hopes of a top 10 finish seemingly extinguished. Victory lifted the Bulldogs to seventh on the ladder.



Arthur Jones shows some dash for the Bulldogs. via Getty Images In a team shorn of Tom Liberatore (soreness) and Riley Garcia (hamstring tightness) and missing Bailey Dale for the first time since 2020, superstar Marcus Bontempelli was a standout. The Bulldogs’ captain ended the game with three goals, 23 disposals, four tackles and five clearances. Matthew Kennedy was the other multiple goalkicker for the visitors, with three, while Bailey Humphrey was busy with 29 disposals and 765 metres gained. For the Suns, Christian Petracca and Leo Lombard kicked two goals each while Touk Miller (39 disposals, five tackles, nine clearances) and Matt Rowell (26 disposals, 11 tackles and eight clearances) were strong in a beaten team.



Suns spearhead Ben King had a tough day, kicking 1.4 and failing to haul in a late mark that could have set up a grandstand finish. AAP Watson and Lewis pile on goals as Hawthorn destroy lowly Tigers Hawthorn have returned to third on the AFL ladder with a major percentage boost thanks to a brutal 70-point demolition of lowly Richmond at the MCG. The Hawks went into the clash sitting sixth after other results this weekend, but their 18.14 (122) to 6.16 (52) thrashing of the Tigers made a major statement and lifted them back into the top four.



Sunday’s final margin flattered Richmond after they kicked several late consolation goals once Hawthorn eased off in the final term. They had led by as much as 87 points during the third quarter. Pointing the way to a win: Hawthorn’s Nick Watson. AFL Photos Uncontracted Hawk Mitch Lewis dominated up forward with five goals, all in the first half. Goalsneak Nick Watson matched him by also kicking five goals in a stunning first-half performance.



The only injury concern for the Hawks was Jack Ginnivan, who was pulled at half-time with the club citing “back soreness.” For Richmond, it was a sour way to commemorate triple premiership player Dion Prestia’s 250th game. The only positive was veteran Tom Lynch finally kicking his 500th goal late in the final term after several weeks stuck on 499. Tiger Taj Hotton failed to finish the game after suffering an ankle injury, while fellow youngster Steely Green finished the match under a HIA. Jarman Impey is fleet of foot and kicks a running goal on Sunday. AFL Photos



Watson, who was back from a two-week injury lay-off, picked up where he left off by kicking the first goal mid-way through the first term after a pedestrian start by both teams. He was able to slot a second goal in the opening quarter but was upstaged by a rampaging Lewis, who kicked three in the first 30 minutes. Lewis would have had four goals by quarter-time had his set shot after the siren not narrowly missed. But Lewis didn’t have to wait too long for his fourth – which came early in the second term – on his way to five majors. The hapless Tigers went goalless in the first term, and were cruelly denied what would have been a brilliant Seth Campbell goal late in the term by an ARC overrule.



Richmond supporters had to wait until the ninth minute of the second quarter to cheer their side’s first major, which came courtesy of Patrick Retschko. View post on X The Tigers had two in a minute after Mykelti Lefau kicked truly, but any joy was short-lived as Hawthorn piled on the next six. Hawthorn led by a whopping 63 points at the main break, their largest halftime lead in five seasons under coach Sam Mitchell. The Hawks threatened to blow the margin beyond 100 points in the third term before the Tigers were able to make the scoreline more respectable by the final siren.



AAP McKay could play through injury for Carlton Scott Spits, Danny Russell Carlton forward Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a minor tear in his meniscus after an awkward clash that commentators described as innocuous-looking against Collingwood at the MCG on Saturday night. Scans on Sunday confirmed the prognosis for McKay, who was forced from the field early in the Blues’ 21-point loss to the Magpies that has effectively ruled Carlton out of the wildcard race.



McKay bumped knees with teammate Sam Walsh early in the first quarter. Despite the benign nature of the impact, McKay was unable to run and took himself from the ground. Harry McKay suffered bone bruising and a meniscus tear. AFL Photos via Getty Images His absence left the Carlton forward line short on potency. The Blues said midfielder Adam Cerra, who experienced hamstring tightness and was withdrawn in the second quarter, had not suffered a strain. Carlton said McKay and Cerra would be tested and both may play against Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium next Saturday. Carlton’s caretaker coach Josh Fraser would not be drawn on the severity of McKay’s injury.



“Those ones can sometimes look worse than what they appear,” Fraser said after the match. “I don’t know. I haven’t received any more information on it.” Fox Footy commentator David King was perplexed by McKay’s injury. “No one is questioning whether he is injured or not,” he said. “We are just wondering if it is a pain issue or is it a structural issue. When it has such an influence on the group, it changes six or seven roles in the team, and they were right in the game.” Collingwood coach Craig McRae agreed McKay’s absence for most of the night aided an undermanned Magpies back line. World.title: Revenge of the discards: How new and improved Tabuai-Fidow buried his old club
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Revenge of the discards: How new and improved Tabuai-Fidow buried his old club Nick Wright Updated July 19, 2026 — 7:07pm ,first published 6:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Bit by bit, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow has sought to evolve his game to thrust his name among the NRL’s upper echelon of fullbacks, and the Dolphins’ superstar added another chapter to that mission in style on Sunday afternoon. Against his former North Queensland Cowboys teammates, ‘The Hammer’ masterminded his side to 36-16 triumph at Suncorp Stadium to cast aside his former life as a lethal running threat who lacked the same work rate and playmaking nous as his rivals. Loading The Queensland Maroons flyer was instrumental in the Dolphins’ first try, holding up his pass for Selwyn Cobbo enough to provide Jamayne Isaako with just enough room to tip-toe down the sideline and complete a remarkable finish in the corner. But it was in the second half when Tabuai-Fidow showcased just how far his playmaking had come, holding up his pass with a double pump brilliantly to once again give Isaako a chance to complete a miraculous put down in the corner.



He finished with 234 running metres, two linebreaks and nine tackle busts. Related Article State of Origin Watch: The moments that prove ‘The Hammer’ is the NRL’s most underrated “When ‘Hammer’s’ playing with confidence he’s got all the skill sets in any game to do those kinds of things, and the best thing about ‘Hammer’ is he’s worked so hard at his craft, and it shows in his confidence out there,” Dolphins co-captain Tom Gilbert said. A desire to blossom into one of rugby league’s leading fullbacks is what forced Tabuai-Fidow away from North Queensland and to Redcliffe, after the Cowboys entrusted Scott Drinkwater as their main man for the No.1 jumper. The latter is now moving to the Dragons, with Jaxon Purdue now viewed as the club’s long-term future.



But Tabuai-Fidow, still just 24 and on track to become the greatest try scorer in State of Origin history, has become one of the game’s more well-rounded custodians – demonstrating a knack for coming up with brilliant try-saving tackles as well as his evolving playmaking strengths. His eight try-assists for the year is already a career-best statistic. Tabuai-Fidow was joined by his fellow former Cowboys Gilbert, Kulikefu Finefeuiaki and Connelly Lemuelu – as well as Felise Kaufusi, who played under-20s for the club – in producing standout performances. The Dolphins celebrate a try. Getty Images Both Gilbert and Kaufusi scored courtesy of silky pass from Kurt Donoghoe, with Gilbert producing his finest performance since making his comeback from a ruptured pec this year.



The Dolphins’ co-captain cut a dejected and embarrassed figure after last week’s 66-0 capitulation against Cronulla, but avenged that with 148 running metres from 17 carries. Finefeuiaki (173 metres, one linebreak) and Lemuelu (142 metres) were also allowed to leave the Cowboys due to the emergence of Jeremiah Nanai and Heilum Luki. But the pair outgunned their old squad mates, with Lemuelu scoring the final try after running onto a short pass from Kodi Nikorima. Dearden’s signs of life amid harsh call His comeback came with it a brutal expense, but the returning Tom Dearden has signalled to the NRL the North Queensland Cowboys can be genuine smokies to clinch the NRL premiership if they can rectify the ball control which cost them on Sunday. Loading



Having been sidelined since round 10 after suffering a syndesmosis injury – a setback which cost him from featuring for Queensland in the State of Origin series – Dearden quickly issued a reminder of the threat he possesses by scoring the first try of the afternoon, and setting up the second with a deft grubber for Nanai. “It felt good to be back out there, and I think performance wise there’s still a bit of rust there and things to work on. I’ll build on that performance,” Dearden said. The 2025 Wally Lewis Medallist was always assured his spot back in the Cowboys fold, but the fact it came at the cost of Jake Clifford was perhaps the harshest calls coach Todd Payten has needed to make this season. Payten’s decision to partner Dearden with young Jaxon Purdue, who has mostly featured in the centres despite coming through the ranks in the halves, appeared to be a hint to the future of what the Cowboys’ long-term playmaking partnership will be. Jamayne Isaako of the Dolphins scores in the corner. Getty Images



It is a move that may have backfired, however, with North Queensland struggling to get in sync after their fast start and unable to manage the contest as the Dolphins attacking began to click into gear. “It was a really difficult decision to be fair, but with the way the game finished last week [one point win against Manly] and the 24 to 48 hours after that I was really worried about him getting his head around playing well,” Payten said. “We had all our back five available, and Jacko’s [Purdue’s] past three weeks were really strong, so it was a decision based on what was best for us this week. We’ll look at the tape, and have a dicussion and make a decision moving forward.” The Katoa void While the Dolphins escaped with the result, some serious attention needs to be put on their fifth-tackle options in the continued absence of halfback Isaiya Katoa.



Mistakes had already cost them defensively – a wayward Brad Schneider pass intercepted by Cowboys’ winger Murray Taulagi in the lead-up to Dearden’s try – and Kristian Woolf’s men were guilty of butchering five chances deep in North Queensland territory across the opening 40 minutes. Three of those came from poor fifth-tackle options as Schneider, Kodi Nikorima and Jeremy Marshall-King all opting to run the ball without much on, rather than search for a kick, while two other chances were curtailed by simple errors. It was initially hoped Katoa would return after next week’s bye to take on the Dragons. However, he now appears more likely a round 23 comeback against the Broncos. Fortunately, the Dolphins’ defence gave them enough time to build into the contest, missing just 24 tackles to the Cowboys’ 55. While that desperation threatened to cost them late as a covering Morgan Knowles forced the ball free from Soni Luke’s arms for Scott Drinkwater to score, it was a far cry from the team who fell apart against the Sharks a week ago in a display which left their premiership credentials on tilt.
